'''Matthew Stephen Leinart''' (born May 11, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for seven seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]], winning the [[Heisman Trophy]] and leading the team to a [[perfect season]] in 2004. Selected 10th overall by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] in the [[2006 NFL draft]], Leinart primarily served as [[Kurt Warner]]'s backup for four seasons. He spent his final three seasons in a backup role for the [[Houston Texans]] and the [[Oakland Raiders]]. Leinart was inducted to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 5, 2017 |title=Rivals Manning, Spurrier enter College Hall of Fame together |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/ncaaf/2017/12/05/rivals-manning-spurrier-enter-college-hall-of-fame-together/108345632/ |access-date=June 21, 2023 |website=USAToday.com |agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

President & CEO | highlights = * 4× [[List of Super Bowl champions|Super Bowl champion]] ([[Super Bowl XV|XV]], [[Super Bowl XVIII|XVIII]], [[Super Bowl XXIV|XXIV]], [[Super Bowl XXVI|XXVI]]) * [[Pro Bowl]] ([[1989 Pro Bowl|1988]]) * First-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] ([[1978 College Football All-America Team|1978]]) * First-team All-East ([[1978 All-East football team|1978]]) * Second-team All-East ([[1979 All-East football team|1979]]) | statlabel1 = [[Interception]]s | statvalue1 = 9 | statlabel2 = [[Quarterback sack|Sacks]] | statvalue2 = 17.0 | statlabel3 = [[Fumble]] recoveries | statvalue3 = 8 | pfr = MillMa01 }} '''Matthew George Millen''' (born March 12, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player and executive in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Millen played as a [[linebacker]] for 12 years for the [[Oakland Raiders|Oakland]] and [[Los Angeles Raiders]], [[San Francisco 49ers]], and [[Washington Redskins]], playing on four [[Super Bowl]]-winning teams and is the only player to win a [[Super Bowl ring]] with three different franchises.[http://www.detroitlions.com/document_display.cfm?document_id=3290 Super Bowl champs on Lions roster] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060317130850/http://www.detroitlions.com/document_display.cfm?document_id=3290 |date=March 17, 2006 }} Detroit Lions.com.[http://www.football.com/cgi-bin/posters/printPost.cgi?pa=yes&category=nflfeature1&PID=2767&at=generic.shtml Lions to stick with Millen by Dan Haugh] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061020044117/http://www.football.com/cgi-bin/posters/printPost.cgi?pa=yes&category=nflfeature1&PID=2767&at=generic.shtml |date=October 20, 2006 }} Football.com. Following his NFL playing career, Millen was a football commentator for several national television and radio networks. His last job before joining the Lions was as a member of the number two broadcast team for ''[[NFL on Fox]]'',[http://www.findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4196/is_19981130/ai_n10470074 Fox's No. 2 announcing team proving itself to be first-rate] The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. and the color commentator for ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' on [[NFL on Westwood One|Westwood One]]. On February 1, 2009, he joined the [[NBC Sports|NBC]] broadcast team for pre-game analysis of [[Super Bowl XLIII]]. He has also been employed by [[ESPN]] as an NFL and college football analyst, and by the [[NFL Network]] as a color commentator on ''[[Thursday Night Football]].''[http://www.freep.com/article/20110505/SPORTS01/110505052/It-s-official-Matt-Millen-out-NFL-Network] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110509070812/http://www.freep.com/article/20110505/SPORTS01/110505052/It-s-official-Matt-Millen-out-NFL-Network|date=May 9, 2011}} In [[2001 Detroit Lions season|2001]], Millen was hired as president and chief executive officer of the [[Detroit Lions]] and served in that position until [[2008 Detroit Lions season|2008]]. His eight-year tenure as head of Detroit Lions led to the worst eight-year record in the history of the modern NFL (31–84, a .270 winning percentage),{{cite web|last=Rank|first=Adam|url=http://www.nfl.com/photoessays/0ap1000000148907/not-so-great-wizards-of-the-nfl|title=Not so great Wizards of the NFL|publisher=[[National Football League]]|date=March 8, 2013|access-date=March 8, 2013}} leading to fan outrage, and ultimately his termination from the franchise on September 24, 2008. Millen assembled the personnel and coaching staff of the [[2008 Detroit Lions season|2008 Lions]], which became the first team to go [[List of winless seasons|0–16]]. It stood as the worst single-season record in NFL history until [[2017 NFL season|2017]], when it was tied by the [[2017 Cleveland Browns season|2017 Cleveland Browns]] who went winless in the season. He is generally regarded among the worst general managers in the history of modern sports.{{Cite web |last=Keri |first=Jonah |date=September 25, 2008 |title=Keri: Worst GMS in sports history - ESPN Page 2 |url=https://www.espn.com/espn/page2/story?page=keri/080925 |access-date=2024-06-27 |website=ESPN.com}} In 2015, Millen returned to broadcasting with [[Fox NFL]] and debuted on the [[Big Ten Network]].

'''Matt O'Dwyer''' (born September 1, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1995 to 2005. He played [[college football]] for the [[Northwestern Wildcats football|Northwestern Wildcats]] and in the NFL for the [[New York Jets]] (1995–1998), the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] (1999–2003), and the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] (2004).<ref>{{cite web | title=Matt O'Dwyer | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/O/ODwyMa20.htm | publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com | accessdate=2009-04-02}}</ref> He blocked on lines that produced a 1,000-yard rusher in seven of his 10 NFL seasons ([[Adrian Murrell]] 1996–1997, [[Curtis Martin]] 1998 and [[Corey Dillon]] 1999–2002). He also helped Dillon to break [[Walter Payton]]'s single-game NFL record, a 278-yard performance vs. [[Denver Broncos|Denver]], October 22, 2000 (since surpassed by [[Jamal Lewis (American football)|Jamal Lewis]] in [[2003 NFL season|2003]] and [[Adrian Peterson]] in [[2007 NFL season|2007]]).

Selected by the Jets as the first pick in the second round (33rd overall) of the [[1995 NFL draft]], O'Dwyer started 64 consecutive games at [[Guard (American football)|guard]] for the Jets (1996–1998) and Bengals (1999).<ref>{{Cite web |title=1995 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1995/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In 2002, he was Cincinnati's only player on the field for every snap. Overall, O'Dwyer played 122 [[regular season]] games (105 [[Starting lineup|starts]]), as well as two [[postseason]] starts, both in 1998 when the Jets nearly advanced to [[Super Bowl XXXIII]]. O'Dwyer was known for his tough style of play; he was one of the most penalized players in the NFL in 1997.<ref>{{cite news |first=Gerald |last=Eskenazi |title=As Push Comes to Shove, O'Dwyer Can't Seem to Hide |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/11/16/sports/pro-football-as-push-comes-to-shove-o-dwyer-can-t-seem-to-hide.html |work=[[New York Times]] |date=November 16, 1997 |accessdate=April 2, 2009 }}</ref> After playing for the Buccaneers in 2004, O'Dwyer was signed by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in 2005, but he was cut at the beginning of the season.<ref>{{cite news |first=Jason |last=Wilde |title=Packers Clear Way For Rookie – Will Whitticker Appears to be the Starting Right Guard as Matt O'Dwyer is Cut |work=[[Wisconsin State Journal]] |date=August 29, 2005 }}</ref> He retired from the NFL on September 1, 2006.<ref>{{cite news |first=Stella |last=Foster |title=Stella's Column |work=[[Chicago Sun-Times]] |date=August 31, 2006 }}</ref> He lives in [[Tampa Bay, Florida|Tampa Bay]] & [[Chicago, Illinois|Chicago]].

O'Dwyer appeared in the [[Jon Favreau]] & [[Vince Vaughn]] movie ''[[Made (2001 film)|Made]]'' with fellow NFL player [[Jason Fabini]] & future ''[[The Sopranos]]'' star [[Federico Castelluccio]] as doormen.

Prater is 13th in NFL history in [[List of most career field goals in NFL history|field goals made]], with 425, and has the second most field goals made by an active NFL player, six shy of [[Nick Folk]]'s 431.

He played [[college football]] for the [[UCF Knights football|UCF Knights]], and was originally signed by the Lions as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2006.
He was cut by the Denver Broncos after completing a suspension for violating the NFL's substance abuse policy. With the Lions in the 2016 and 2017 seasons, Prater set the NFL records for consecutive field goal conversions of 50+ yards (14 field goals) and 55+ yards (seven field goals).
